title: Detection of Domain Properties
summary: This detection strategy covers the reconnaissance technique of gathering domain property information, where an adversary looks up registration details, name servers, and hosting for your domains. It matters because those details expose who owns and hosts your infrastructure, how old a domain is, and which provider to impersonate or attack next. The telemetry that makes detection possible is resolver and authoritative name server logs, web proxy records of lookups to registration and reputation services, and certificate transparency records that reveal newly registered names similar to your brand. The main failure mode is that most registration and reputation lookups are made by legitimate security, marketing, and mail hygiene tools, so the rule needs an approved service baseline before it can be trusted.

beginner.definition: This detection watches for people who look up the registration details of your internet domains. A domain is the name people type to reach a website, such as example. Registration details include the owner, the name servers, and the hosting provider. The rule looks for unusual lookups of those details from inside or outside your network.
beginner.whyItMatters: Registration details tell an attacker who runs your systems and where they are hosted. That knowledge helps them pick a target that looks real. It also helps them build a lookalike domain that staff may trust. Catching the lookups early gives you time to protect your brand.
howItWorks: The resolver or authoritative name server records each query it receives.
The web proxy records requests to registration and reputation lookup services.
The rule watches for lookup requests that name your own domains or close variations.
It counts how many different lookup services one source uses in a short window.
Certificate transparency records show new certificates for lookalike names.
A pattern that mixes several record types with reputation lookups raises an alert.
beginner.example: Imagine a library sign in sheet where visitors write the book they want. Someone may ask for the address of your building. The same visitor may ask for the manager name and the opening hours. That visitor is collecting facts, not reading. One question is normal. The pattern of many related questions from one visitor is what the librarian notes down.
takeaways: Domain property lookups often mix name queries with reputation and registration services.
Lookalike domain registration is the outcome worth catching early.
A baseline of approved lookup services is required before alerts are useful.

objectives: Explain what domain property information includes and why it is collected.
Name the logs that record registration and reputation lookups.
Write a rule that flags combined mapping and reputation lookups.
Describe how lookalike domain registration shows up in transparency logs.
Reduce noise using an approved service and scanner baseline.
dataSources: Recursive DNS resolver query logs recording queried name, record type and client source address for registration and reputation service names
Authoritative name server query logs for organization owned zones including delegation and mail record requests
Web proxy and secure web gateway logs showing requests to domain registration and reputation lookup endpoints
Certificate transparency records for newly issued certificates whose names are close variations of organization domains
logic: The pattern is a source combining classic record lookups for your domains with requests to registration or reputation services, or a burst of lookups for domain names that closely copy your brand. The fields that must be correlated are the queried or requested domain, the record type, the lookup service, the source address, and the count of distinct names per source in a time window. The malicious case is an outside source listing your name servers and registration details and then checking the reputation of lookalike names it intends to register. The benign case is a mail hygiene or brand monitoring service that performs the same lookups on a documented schedule from approved ranges.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Domain Registration and Reputation Lookup Activity
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: dns
# detection:
#   selection:
#     query|endswith:
#       - '.example[.]com'
#     query_type:
#       - 'SOA'
#       - 'NS'
#       - 'TXT'
#   filter_approved:
#     src_ip|contains:
#       - '10[.]0[.]'
#       - '192[.]0[.]2[.]'
#   condition: selection and not filter_approved | count(query) by src_ip > 20 within 10m
# level: low
falsePositives: Email authentication checks that read sender policy and domain key records for every inbound message
Brand protection and takedown services that monitor lookalike domains on a daily schedule
Marketing teams that audit domain delegation during a website migration project
tuningNotes: Baseline every service and internal host that queries your domains or registration endpoints for two weeks and filter those sources, then scope the rule to queries from outside ranges and to lookalike name patterns. Keep a separate long window count of distinct sources per domain so that slow collection still surfaces, and raise priority when a lookalike name is registered or certified shortly after. The coverage you lose is an attacker who uses public resolvers and hosted lookup services, which hides the original client from your logs.
